title: Tetzaveh: beaten olives (Exodus 27:20)
hook: the eternal lamp burns pure oil from crushed olives

segments.voice: Yesterday Terumah ended with the ark's poles, never taken out. Your line was ready to travel. What did you make ready? Today, a new portion, and a lamp that never goes out. Day three hundred fifty-eight.

Walk into almost any synagogue in the world, at any hour, and look up above the ark where the Torah scrolls are kept. There's a small light burning there. Sometimes it's an old brass lamp, sometimes a modern fixture, sometimes a simple electric bulb. It's on when the room is full and when it's empty. It's on at three in the morning. It's called the ner tamid, and its story starts in this week's portion, with an instruction about olives, and about how they had to be treated to give the purest light.
screen: `A LIGHT ABOVE THE ARK.` → `ON AT THREE IN THE MORNING.` → `IT STARTS WITH OLIVES.`

segments.voice: The portion is called Tetzaveh, you shall command, from its first verse. In the old Jewish translation: "And thou shalt command the children of Israel, that they bring unto thee pure olive oil beaten for the light, to cause a lamp to burn continually." A lamp continually: in Hebrew, ner tamid. In the wilderness sanctuary it meant the menorah, lit from evening to morning, every night, without a gap. Today every synagogue keeps its own ner tamid as a reminder. Now look at the oil. Pure olive oil, beaten. Rashi explains: the olives were crushed gently in a mortar, and only the first drops were used for the light. That first oil is the clearest, with the least sediment, so it burns bright and clean. The rest could go to other uses. The rabbis saw a picture in this. The prophet Jeremiah once called Israel a leafy olive tree. And a midrash says: just as an olive gives its oil only after it's beaten and crushed, so Israel, through hard times, has given light. That's a strong image, and it should be handled carefully. This midrash doesn't say suffering is good, or that pain is something to wish for. It says something more modest and more hopeful. Sometimes, after being crushed, a person or a people gives off a light they didn't know they had. A widow who starts a support group. A survivor who becomes a teacher. The pain wasn't the point. The light was what they made of it.
screen: `TETZAVEH: YOU SHALL COMMAND.` · `PURE OLIVE OIL BEATEN FOR THE LIGHT.` · `RASHI: THE FIRST, CLEAREST DROPS.` · `CRUSHED, THEN GIVING LIGHT.` · then, large: `CRUSHED OLIVES GIVE LIGHT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: honor a light that came from pain. Settle, and breathe. Think of someone you know who went through something crushing and came out giving light to others. A friend who now helps people through the same thing. A grandparent whose hard life made them gentle. Maybe it's you. Don't make the pain smaller than it was. Just notice the light, and honor it. If you pray, you can give thanks for that person. The bell holds the time.
Ner tamid. The lamp that burns continually: once in the sanctuary, fed with oil from crushed olives, and now above the ark in every synagogue.
Your line: crushed olives give light. Today, tell one person whose hard road made them a light for others that you see it. Day three hundred fifty-eight.

screen: `DAY 358 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: TETZAVEH: MOSES' NAME IS MISSING.`

howItsDone: Synagogues keep a ner tamid, an eternal light, burning above or before the ark that holds the Torah scrolls, recalling the lamp of the wilderness sanctuary; today it is usually electric.

options: the first drops from olives crushed in a mortar.

original.note: Hebrew: a lamp continually, the eternal light.

trapdoor: what you thought: a light that's always switched on.
what it means: a lamp fed with oil from crushed olives; light that comes after pressure.
what a scholar hears: Shemot Rabbah 36:1 links Exodus 27:20 to Jeremiah 11:16: as the olive is beaten to give oil, so Israel.

sources.quoted: And thou shalt command the children of Israel, that they bring unto thee pure olive oil beaten for the light, to cause a lamp to burn continually.

notes: Exodus 27:20 quoted from JPS 1917 from memory (KJV reads 'that they bring thee pure oil olive beaten'); verify JPS wording carefully.
Rashi on 27:20: 'katit' – crushed in a mortar, first drop for the menorah; the rest for meal-offerings. Confirm.
Shemot Rabbah 36:1: Israel compared to the olive (Jeremiah 11:16), which gives oil only when beaten. Confirm wording and section.
The script frames suffering carefully ('this midrash doesn't say suffering is good'); a Keeper may want to nuance (some sources do speak of yissurin shel ahavah).
Wilderness ner tamid: the menorah lit from evening to morning (27:21); some commentators identify the ner tamid with the western lamp. Simplified.
